questions.stem: The day after the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933, the Reichstag Fire Decree:
options: gave Hitler's cabinet the power to pass laws without the Reichstag for four years
merged the offices of Chancellor and President into the single office of Führer
removed German citizenship from Jews and banned their marriage to other Germans
suspended civil liberties such as freedom of speech, the press and assembly
questions.explanation: Hindenburg's emergency decree, issued under Article 48, suspended basic rights and allowed arrest without trial, and thousands of Communists were detained. The power to legislate without the Reichstag came with the Enabling Act in March.

questions.stem: In the Reichstag election of 5 March 1933, held after the Reichstag fire, the Nazi Party:
options: lost seats to the Communists, who became the largest party in the Reichstag
did not take part because Hindenburg had banned all parties from standing
won about 44% of the vote and needed its conservative allies for a majority
won over two-thirds of the vote and could change the constitution on its own
questions.explanation: Even with intimidation of opponents, the Nazis won about 44%, so they relied on the nationalist DNVP for a majority. A two-thirds majority for the Enabling Act was secured only by excluding the Communists and winning over the Centre Party.

questions.stem: How did the Nazis secure the two-thirds majority needed to pass the Enabling Act on 23 March 1933?
options: Hindenburg ordered all deputies to vote for it under his Article 48 powers
the Nazis had won a two-thirds majority on their own in the March election
Communist deputies were barred or arrested, and the Centre Party voted in favour
the Social Democrats agreed to support it in return for two seats in Hitler's cabinet
questions.explanation: With the KPD deputies absent and SA men around the Kroll Opera House, the Centre Party voted yes after promises about the Church. Only the SPD voted against, and the act passed 444 to 94.

questions.stem: The Nazi process of 'Gleichschaltung' (coordination) in 1933 involved:
options: returning the powers of the federal states that the Weimar Republic had removed
coordinating German foreign policy with the League of Nations in Geneva
bringing all political, social and cultural organisations under Nazi control
sharing power equally between the Nazi Party and the other German parties
questions.explanation: Coordination meant Nazifying institutions: state governments were taken over, trade unions abolished on 2 May 1933, other parties dissolved and clubs and professions brought into Nazi bodies. By July 1933 Germany was legally a one-party state.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events in 1933 is in the correct order?
options: Hitler appointed Chancellor; one-party law; Reichstag fire; trade unions abolished
Enabling Act; trade unions abolished; law making the Nazis the only legal party
Trade unions abolished; Enabling Act; Reichstag fire; Hitler appointed Chancellor
Law making the Nazis the only legal party; Reichstag fire; Enabling Act passed
questions.explanation: The Enabling Act was passed in March, unions were abolished on 2 May, and the Law against the Formation of New Parties of 14 July made the Nazis the only legal party. Hitler's appointment in January and the fire in February came first.

questions.stem: Why did Hitler move against Ernst Röhm and the SA leadership in the Night of the Long Knives (30 June to 2 July 1934)?
options: The SA had refused to take part in the boycott of Jewish businesses in April 1933
Hindenburg had ordered the SA to be dissolved and threatened to dismiss Hitler
The army saw the SA as a rival, and Röhm's talk of a 'second revolution' alarmed elites
Röhm had secretly led the Communist opposition to the Enabling Act and organised strikes
questions.explanation: Röhm wanted the SA to absorb the army and spoke of a second, social revolution, worrying the generals and business. The SS killed Röhm and other SA leaders, along with opponents such as Kurt von Schleicher, which won the army's support.

questions.stem: On Hindenburg's death in August 1934, Hitler combined the offices of Chancellor and President. Why was the army's oath that followed especially significant?
options: Soldiers swore to obey the Reichstag, which kept a check on Hitler's new power
Soldiers swore loyalty to the Kaiser, signalling a coming return of the monarchy
Soldiers swore to defend the Treaty of Versailles and its limits on the army
Soldiers swore personal loyalty to Hitler, not to the constitution or the state
questions.explanation: The oath bound soldiers to Hitler personally, which later made many officers feel unable to act against him. Together with a plebiscite in which about 90% voted yes, it completed the consolidation of his power.

questions.stem: The Nazi idea of the 'Volksgemeinschaft' was:
options: a parliament of elected representatives from every German social class
a people's community of racially defined Germans united above class
a federation of the German states each keeping its own laws and army
an economic plan to share all private property equally among workers
questions.explanation: The people's community promised to replace class and party divisions with national unity, but it was racially defined, so Jews and others labelled 'alien' were excluded. Propaganda, KdF holidays and the Winter Relief collections promoted the idea.

questions.stem: The Nazi concept of 'Lebensraum' referred to:
options: building new housing estates for German workers in the industrial cities
moving German farmers from the east into the industrial Ruhr valley
returning Germany's overseas colonies that had been lost in 1919
gaining living space for Germans through expansion into eastern Europe
questions.explanation: Lebensraum, set out in Mein Kampf, meant conquering land in the east, especially from Poland and the USSR, for German settlement. It linked racial ideology to plans for war.

questions.stem: The 'Führerprinzip' (leader principle) meant that:
options: Hitler shared his authority equally with the cabinet and the Reichstag
the army's generals chose the leader of the nation from their own ranks
authority flowed down from Hitler, whose will stood above the law
leaders at every level were elected by the members they directed
questions.explanation: Under the leader principle each level obeyed the one above, with Hitler's will as the final authority, replacing elections and debate. It also encouraged officials to compete to anticipate what Hitler wanted.

questions.stem: Historian Hans Mommsen described Hitler as a 'weak dictator', while Ian Kershaw argued that officials were 'working towards the Führer'. Kershaw's idea suggests that:
options: the regime was run by the army, with Hitler acting only as a figurehead
Hitler had no ideas of his own and simply followed public opinion polls
officials radicalised policy by anticipating what they believed Hitler wanted
Hitler personally drafted every single law and decree that the regime ever issued
questions.explanation: Kershaw combined the intentionalist and structuralist views: Hitler's ideological goals set the direction, while competing officials pushed policy further to win his favour. Mommsen stressed the chaotic, competing structure of the regime rather than Hitler's control.

questions.stem: On 1 April 1933 the Nazi regime organised:
options: a nationwide boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers
the first deportation of German Jews to camps in Poland
the exclusion of all Jewish children from every German school
a law requiring Jews to add the names Israel or Sara
questions.explanation: SA men stood outside Jewish businesses to discourage customers. The boycott had mixed public support and lasted only a day, but it marked the start of official action against Jews. Exclusion from schools came after Kristallnacht in 1938.

questions.stem: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of April 1933 affected Jewish Germans by:
options: requiring every Jewish-owned business to be sold to a non-Jewish German owner
taking away the German citizenship of Jews born outside the country
forcing all Jewish civil servants to emigrate within three months
removing most Jewish officials, teachers and judges from public employment
questions.explanation: The law dismissed Jews and political opponents from the civil service, which included teachers and judges, though at first Hindenburg secured exemptions for Jewish war veterans. The forced sale of businesses ('Aryanisation') was pressed hardest in 1938.

questions.stem: Under the Nuremberg Laws of September 1935:
options: Jewish emigration from Germany was made illegal and borders were closed
all Jewish property was seized and transferred directly to the Nazi Party itself
Jews lost Reich citizenship and marriage between Jews and non-Jews was banned
Jews were forced to live in sealed ghettos in the major German cities
questions.explanation: The Reich Citizenship Law made Jews subjects without political rights, and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour banned marriages and relationships with non-Jews. Supplementary decrees defined who counted as a Jew by ancestry.

questions.stem: After the violence of Kristallnacht on 9-10 November 1938, the regime:
options: banned the SA and SS from taking part in any further actions against German Jews
lifted the Nuremberg Laws to calm foreign criticism before the Munich Conference
arrested about 30,000 Jewish men and fined the Jewish community one billion Reichsmarks
publicly apologised for the damage and paid full compensation to the Jewish owners of property
questions.explanation: Tens of thousands of Jewish men were sent to concentration camps, the Jewish community was made to pay a collective fine, and insurance payments were seized by the state. Jews were then pushed out of the economy and schools. The Munich Conference had already taken place in September.

questions.stem: At the Évian Conference of July 1938, representatives of 32 countries, including Australia, met to discuss Jewish refugees from Germany and Austria. Its main outcome was that:
options: most countries, including Australia, would not substantially increase refugee intake
Germany agreed to stop its persecution of Jews in return for foreign loans
the participating nations agreed to accept every single Jewish refugee who applied to them
the League of Nations set up a Jewish homeland in Palestine immediately
questions.explanation: Nearly every delegation expressed sympathy but offered few places, which Nazi propaganda exploited. Australia later announced a quota of 15,000 refugees over three years, but the war interrupted it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the overall pattern of Nazi policy towards Jewish people from 1933 to 1939?
options: Escalation: boycott and dismissals, then loss of citizenship, then violence and dispossession
Steady easing: early violence was replaced by toleration once the Olympic Games had ended
Constant policy: every measure against Jews was announced together in January 1933
Local policy only: national law never mentioned Jews, and actions came only from local mobs
questions.explanation: Policy moved through stages: the 1933 boycott and dismissals, the 1935 Nuremberg Laws, and the 1938 Kristallnacht violence and forced 'Aryanisation'. Visible antisemitism was briefly toned down for the 1936 Olympics, then intensified.

questions.stem: The Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring of July 1933 introduced:
options: interest-free marriage loans for couples who could prove their 'Aryan' descent
compulsory sterilisation of people with conditions judged to be hereditary
free health checks for all German children before they started school
a ban on Jewish doctors treating non-Jewish patients in German hospitals
questions.explanation: Hereditary health courts ordered the sterilisation of people with conditions such as schizophrenia, epilepsy and supposed 'feeble-mindedness'. It reflected the Nazi belief in racial hygiene and led towards the murder of disabled people that began in 1939.

questions.stem: Which group was persecuted by the Nazi regime mainly because its members refused to give the Hitler salute, swear loyalty oaths or serve in the military?
options: Lutheran pastors of the German Christians
members of the Hitler Youth
Catholic priests under the Concordat
Jehovah's Witnesses
questions.explanation: Jehovah's Witnesses refused on religious grounds to salute Hitler or perform military service, and many were imprisoned in concentration camps. The German Christians were the pro-Nazi Protestant movement.

questions.stem: Nazi ideology saw the main role of German women as:
options: serving in front-line units of the army alongside German men
entering the professions to replace the dismissed Jewish lawyers
leading the Nazi Party at national level as Reich ministers
bearing and raising children and caring for the home and family
questions.explanation: The slogan 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche' summed up the ideal of women as mothers and homemakers. Marriage loans, the Mother's Cross and propaganda encouraged large families, while women were barred from becoming judges or lawyers.

questions.stem: Under the Honour Cross of the German Mother, introduced in 1938, a mother of eight or more children was awarded:
options: the gold cross
the bronze cross
the silver cross
the iron cross
questions.explanation: The cross was awarded in bronze for four or five children, silver for six or seven and gold for eight or more, to 'racially valuable' mothers. The Iron Cross is a military decoration.

questions.stem: Statistics show that the number of women in paid work in Germany rose in the late 1930s. How does this challenge a simple reading of Nazi policy on women?
options: It shows that the marriage loan scheme was never actually introduced
It shows that women had won the right to vote for the first time in 1938
Rearmament created labour shortages that overrode the ideal of women at home
It proves that Nazi ideology had always encouraged German women to join the army
questions.explanation: Ideology pushed women out of some jobs in 1933, but rearmament and the Four-Year Plan created shortages of labour, so women's employment grew. Practice and ideology diverged. German women had voted since 1919.

questions.stem: From 1936 the Hitler Youth Law made the Hitler Youth:
options: a voluntary club that only the children of party members could join
a branch of the army that sent its older members to the front line
a church youth group run jointly by the Catholic and Protestant churches
the official state youth organisation, alongside home and school
questions.explanation: The December 1936 law made the Hitler Youth, with the League of German Girls (BDM), the official youth organisation, and membership became compulsory in 1939. Rival youth groups, including many church groups, were closed down or absorbed.

questions.stem: How did the Nazi regime change school education after 1933?
options: It left the curriculum unchanged and allowed teachers to choose their own textbooks
It abolished schools entirely and placed all education in the hands of the Hitler Youth
It required every child to attend a church school run by the Catholic clergy
It added race science and more physical training, and pressed teachers to join a Nazi league
questions.explanation: Curricula stressed race science, German history and biology from a racial view, and physical education received more time. Teachers were vetted and most joined the National Socialist Teachers' League. Schools continued alongside the Hitler Youth.

questions.stem: After the abolition of trade unions in May 1933, German workers were organised into:
options: independent unions elected by factory workers
the German Labour Front (DAF), led by Robert Ley
the Reich Food Estate, led by Walther Darré
the Confessing Church's workers' councils
questions.explanation: The DAF replaced the unions and included employers and workers, but workers lost the right to strike or bargain over wages. Its sections Strength Through Joy and Beauty of Labour aimed to win workers' loyalty.

questions.stem: Registered unemployment in Germany fell from about six million in early 1933 to very low levels by 1939. Which factor would a historian need to consider in evaluating this as evidence of Nazi economic success?
options: Rearmament, conscription and the exclusion of many women and Jews from the figures
The introduction of a forty-hour week with sharply rising real wages for all workers
The ending of rearmament in 1935 and the shift of spending to consumer goods
Large loans from the USA under the Dawes Plan that funded new public housing
questions.explanation: Job creation schemes, the Reich Labour Service, conscription from 1935 and rearmament absorbed workers, and some groups were removed from the statistics. Real wages stayed low and hours lengthened; the Dawes Plan was a Weimar policy.

questions.stem: Under the Volkswagen savings scheme, German workers paid weekly instalments towards a 'people's car'. What happened to the cars?
options: The cars were delivered only to Nazi Party members and SS officers in the end
The scheme was cancelled in 1936 and all of the workers' savings were repaid with interest
None reached the savers before the war, as the factory turned to military production
Every saver received a car by 1938, making Germany the most motorised nation in Europe
questions.explanation: Hundreds of thousands of workers saved, but no cars reached them before the war, and the factory turned to military production once war began. The scheme shows the gap between Nazi promises to workers and reality.

questions.stem: Which Nazi minister headed the Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda from March 1933?
options: Hermann Göring
Rudolf Hess
Joseph Goebbels
Heinrich Himmler
questions.explanation: Goebbels controlled the press, radio, film and the arts, and through the Reich Chamber of Culture decided who could work in them. Himmler led the SS and the police.

questions.stem: The concentration camp at Dachau, opened in March 1933, was used at first mainly to hold:
options: Jewish children removed from German schools after Kristallnacht
political opponents of the regime, especially Communists and Social Democrats
French prisoners of war captured during the remilitarisation of the Rhineland
foreign workers recruited for the regime's rearmament program
questions.explanation: Dachau, set up by Himmler near Munich, held political prisoners taken into 'protective custody' without trial and became a model for later camps. Arrests of Jews in large numbers came later, notably after Kristallnacht.

questions.stem: Robert Gellately's study of Gestapo files found that the Gestapo had relatively few officers. What does his research suggest about how the regime controlled society?
options: The Gestapo had little effect because Germans ignored its instructions
Control depended entirely on the army rather than on the police
The regime relied on foreign intelligence services to watch Germans
Much of its information came from denunciations by ordinary Germans
questions.explanation: Gellately showed that many Gestapo cases began with tips from neighbours, colleagues or family, often for personal motives. This suggests a degree of popular participation and consent, alongside fear, rather than an all-seeing police force.

questions.stem: The regime promoted the cheap 'People's Receiver' radio and broadcast Hitler's speeches. A historian could best use sales figures for the radio as evidence of:
options: the content of foreign radio stations heard by German listeners
how far the regime's broadcasts could reach into German homes
how far Germans privately believed the messages that they heard
the number of Germans who joined the Nazi Party after 1933
questions.explanation: Sales figures show the potential reach of propaganda but not whether listeners were persuaded. Belief needs other evidence, such as diaries, Sopade reports or Gestapo reports on public mood.

questions.stem: Leni Riefenstahl's film Triumph of the Will (1935) records the 1934 Nuremberg Rally. For a historian of the Nazi regime it is most valuable as evidence of:
options: the true level of support for the regime among all Germans
the planning of the Night of the Long Knives earlier that year
the image of unity and leadership the regime wanted to project
the private feelings of the many ordinary Germans who took part
questions.explanation: The film was carefully staged and edited to show a disciplined nation devoted to Hitler, so it is strong evidence of propaganda aims and methods. It cannot show how participants or the wider population really felt.

questions.stem: Historians debate whether the Nazi regime rested mainly on terror or on consent. Which pair of sources would best help test this question?
options: Mein Kampf and the 1920 Nazi Party program with its 25 points
The Treaty of Versailles and the Weimar Constitution, both of 1919
Triumph of the Will and a Nazi election poster from 1932
Gestapo case files and exiled SPD (Sopade) reports on public morale
questions.explanation: Gestapo files show how repression worked and who informed, while Sopade reports from underground contacts record grumbling, conformity and support. The other pairs show Nazi aims or propaganda, or come from before 1933.

questions.stem: The Confessing Church, formed in 1934 by Protestant pastors such as Martin Niemöller, opposed:
options: the Concordat between the Vatican and the Nazi state signed in July 1933
all of Hitler's foreign policy, including rearmament and the 1935 Saar plebiscite
the Weimar Constitution and the right of women to vote in elections
Nazi attempts to control the Protestant Church and impose Nazi doctrine on it
questions.explanation: Through the Barmen Declaration of 1934 the Confessing Church rejected the pro-Nazi German Christians and state control of the Church. Its opposition was mainly religious rather than a political campaign; Niemöller was arrested in 1937 and held in camps until 1945.

questions.stem: In 1937 Pope Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge ('With burning concern'), read from Catholic pulpits in Germany:
options: criticised Nazi breaches of the Concordat and racial ideology
called on all German Catholics to overthrow Hitler's government
praised the Nuremberg Laws as a defence of the German family
ended the Concordat and withdrew the papal nuncio from Berlin
questions.explanation: The encyclical, smuggled into Germany and read on Palm Sunday 1937, condemned the regime's violations of the Concordat and its idolisation of race and state. It did not call for revolt, and the Concordat remained in force.

questions.stem: Historian Detlev Peukert described a scale of dissent in Nazi Germany from nonconformity, through refusal and protest, to resistance. Where would young people listening to banned swing music fit on this scale?
options: Protest: a public campaign of strikes to win back the legal right to free trade unions
Refusal: official refusal by the army high command to obey orders from Hitler
Nonconformity: rejecting Nazi norms in daily life without aiming to topple the regime
Resistance: an organised attempt to overthrow the regime by force of arms
questions.explanation: The Swing Youth rejected Nazi culture and the Hitler Youth, but their aim was personal freedom, not the overthrow of the regime. Peukert's scale helps historians avoid treating all dissent as resistance.

questions.stem: On 8 November 1939 Georg Elser attempted to kill Hitler by:
options: shooting at Hitler's car during the parade for the Berlin Olympics
planting a time bomb in a pillar at the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich
leading a group of army officers in a coup during the Sudeten crisis
organising a general strike of workers in the factories of the Ruhr
questions.explanation: Elser, a carpenter acting alone, hid a bomb in the beer hall where Hitler spoke each year, but Hitler left early and the bomb killed others. The officers' conspiracy of 1938, involving Ludwig Beck, was a separate plan that was abandoned after Munich.

questions.stem: Victor Klemperer, a Jewish academic in Dresden, kept a diary from 1933 to 1945. Which is the greatest strength of the diary as a source on the impact of Nazi policies on Jewish people?
options: It records his experience of each new restriction as it happened, without hindsight
It was written for publication by the Propaganda Ministry and is therefore an official record
It gives a complete statistical record of all Jewish emigration from Germany
It was written after 1945, so it includes the knowledge of what happened later
questions.explanation: Written at the time, the diary shows how measures such as dismissal, loss of property and bans on daily activities affected one person and those around him. Its limitation is that it reflects one man's position and experience.

questions.stem: A memoir published in the 1960s by a former senior Nazi official claims he knew nothing about the persecution of Jews. A historian would treat this claim with caution mainly because:
options: senior Nazi officials were not allowed to keep diaries during the 1930s
the persecution of Jews began only after the war ended in 1945
the author had a strong motive to minimise his own responsibility after 1945
memoirs never contain any accurate information about the people and events involved
questions.explanation: Postwar memoirs by former Nazis were often written to protect the author's reputation, so claims of ignorance need to be checked against contemporary documents. Memoirs can still be useful for other details, so they are not worthless.
